guides.title: Reading crowded patterns without rushing your taps
guides.description: Separate visual density from movement speed and practise following object order at different approach rates.

sections.title: Identify the point where the pattern becomes unclear
sections.body: Watch the lead-in to a difficult section. Can you describe the next few objects in order, including slider endings and direction changes? If not, begin with recognition rather than assuming your cursor is too slow. A replay shows inputs and movement, not eye tracking: a late movement can suggest several causes and does not prove a reading problem.

sections.title: AR and timing difficulty are different controls
sections.body: Approach rate changes how early objects become visible. Lower AR gives more advance visibility but can leave more objects on screen together; higher AR gives less advance visibility. Overall difficulty controls judgement windows. Changing AR is therefore not the same as making tapping timing more forgiving. Rate-changing mods also change the real time available, so retain the exact settings in comparisons.

sections.title: Practice: recognise, then execute
sections.body: Suggested exercise: choose a comfortable map containing one crowded section. Watch it once and identify the object order, then play it without pausing. If necessary, adjust AR slightly while keeping rate fixed and test whether the ordering becomes clearer. Do not simultaneously change your skin, tablet area and rate. After a few attempts, return to the original AR and try an unfamiliar map with a similar density.

sections.title: Measure something beyond memorisation
sections.body: Record whether the first error occurs before, during or after the crowded section. Compare first attempts on several maps, not only a section you have repeated many times. If only the rehearsed map improves, add unfamiliar patterns at the same demand. If you recognise the order but still click before arriving, move your focus to aim-tap coordination rather than continuing to lower AR.

guides.title: Low accuracy: read timing bias and unstable rate together
guides.description: Understand the difference between consistently early inputs and inconsistent timing before changing your settings.

sections.title: A tight group can still be off-centre
sections.body: Unstable rate measures the spread of hit errors, not whether their average is centred on the intended time. It is ten times the standard deviation of hit errors measured in milliseconds. Consistently late hits can therefore produce a low UR and poor accuracy. Check average error and the distribution alongside UR; do not interpret a single smaller number as proof that every part of timing improved.

sections.title: Compare compatible measurements
sections.body: Use the same client, mods, rate and object selection. Stable's rate-mod UR convention and modern lazer's real-time UR convention differ; do not apply a conversion twice. Also check OD: identical input errors can produce different judgement counts under tighter windows. A partial failed play and a full completion may cover very different sections even when they share a map title.

sections.title: Practice: contrast simple and complex rhythms
sections.body: Suggested exercise: choose a familiar map with simple rhythms and a second map with rhythm changes at a manageable speed. Keep settings unchanged and record several attempts. If the simple rhythm stays centred but the complex pattern spreads out, practise recognising and executing those transitions. If both shift consistently to one side across multiple maps, investigate the setup and your timing reference before deciding that a harder map is the solution.

sections.title: Do not calibrate from one bad play
sections.body: Avoid repeatedly adjusting offset after individual misses. Write down the original setting before any controlled change, then compare multiple familiar maps under otherwise identical conditions. Keep the change only when it improves the repeatable bias without introducing another problem. If the evidence is mixed, restore the baseline. A wide distribution is not fixed merely by moving its centre.

guides.title: Slider breaks: check the head, follow and exit separately
guides.description: Find whether slider mistakes happen on entry, during tracking or when moving to the next object.

sections.title: Locate the failed event
sections.body: Begin with the exact judgement and the client rules used for that play. A slider contains more than its starting circle, and a failed slider event should not automatically be described as a missed head. Inspect cursor movement and held inputs through the relevant part. When only a summary score is available, keep the cause unresolved rather than inventing a tracking diagnosis.

sections.title: Look at the transition as well as the slider
sections.body: If the same slider repeatedly breaks, review the preceding object and the next target. Did the cursor arrive late, cut a curve, leave while input was still required, or move correctly but release? These observations lead to different exercises. An apparently easy slider may be difficult because of how you enter or leave it, not because its shape alone is demanding.

sections.title: Practice: keep the exit in the exercise
sections.body: Suggested exercise: repeat a short section containing the preceding object, the entire slider and the next few objects. Focus first on completing the slider, then inspect whether the next input remains on time. If you slow the section, keep its geometry unchanged and return to the original rate afterwards. Do not practise only the slider in isolation and assume its transition is solved.

sections.title: Check that you did not move the error
sections.body: Count slider-event failures and errors immediately after the slider across several attempts. Fewer slider breaks accompanied by more late next-object misses is a tradeoff, not a completed fix. Test another slider with a comparable exit direction. Keep stable, lazer and Classic settings separate so a scoring-rule change is not mistaken for a technique improvement.

sources.title: osu! help centre: Upgrading to lazer

guides.title: Good sections, inconsistent full plays: build consistency
guides.description: Compare section practice with complete attempts and identify repeatable breakdowns without relying only on personal bests.

sections.title: Separate a fixed obstacle from scattered misses
sections.body: Compare several complete attempts on the same setup. Repeated failures at one transition suggest a focused practice target. Misses distributed across otherwise manageable sections call for a broader comparison. Do not conclude that scattered misses are nerves or fatigue from the score alone; those explanations need more context than a replay can provide.

sections.title: Track opportunities, not just errors
sections.body: A section missed three times in three attempts is different from one missed three times in thirty attempts. Record how often you actually reached each section. Attempts that ended earlier should not count as successful runs through a later pattern. Keep the first-error location and completion status alongside accuracy so your review does not reward repeated early retries.

sections.title: Practice: alternate sections and full attempts
sections.body: Suggested exercise: take one baseline full attempt, practise a troublesome transition briefly, then return to a full attempt. Include the lead-in when isolating the section. Keep another map with similar demands in the session so you can test transfer. Use a small planned block rather than continuing until a lucky full combo hides the less consistent attempts.

sections.title: Judge your typical play
sections.body: Compare the middle result and the range of results across similar sessions, as well as your best. A narrower spread of miss counts or more frequent clean transitions can be useful progress before a new personal best appears. If your isolated success does not survive a full play, extend the lead-in or practise entering the section from different contexts rather than only adding repetitions.

guides.title: Choose maps for practice, score targets and skill checks
guides.description: Build a useful map pool by distinguishing maps you want to score on from maps that expose a specific weakness.

sections.title: Give each map a job
sections.body: Use a score target to seek a strong result with skills you can already repeat. Use a practice target to expose one manageable weakness. Use a check map to test whether an improvement transfers without extensive rehearsal. One map can change roles over time, but mixing these goals within every attempt makes it harder to decide whether a session helped.

sections.title: Inspect the difficulty, not only its star badge
sections.body: A beatmapset contains distinct difficulties; compare the exact difficulty you intend to play. Star rating alone does not describe every demand you will experience. Preview the relevant sections and compare spacing, rhythm, burst length, direction changes and transitions. Keep AR, OD and rate in view rather than assuming that equal stars make two maps equivalent practice.

sections.title: Practice: build a three-map pool
sections.body: Suggested exercise: choose one familiar score target, one map with a repeated weakness and one less familiar map with a similar demand. Record the exact difficulty and mods for each. Play the check map before rehearsing it extensively. Replace a practice map when you can repeat the target section reliably, or when it combines so many failures that you cannot identify a useful focus.

sections.title: Use PP scenarios without treating them as predictions
sections.body: PP at a chosen accuracy describes a score scenario with additional assumptions such as combo and misses. An SS value is not the amount you should expect to earn, and score PP is not the same as profile gain. On the website, use these scenarios to compare potential results. Use your actual recent performance and in-app compatibility evidence to judge whether the scenario is realistic for you.

guides.title: Stuck at the same level? Review the evidence before changing everything
guides.description: Use recent attempts to distinguish a score plateau from a repeated skill problem and plan a controlled change.

sections.title: Define what has stopped improving
sections.body: No new top PP score does not necessarily mean that nothing improved. Compare completion rate, section accuracy and repeated errors on familiar demands. Conversely, one personal best does not establish that your typical play improved. Choose a recent review period and keep the map and settings comparable; a year's worth of very different plays can obscure the problem you have now.

sections.title: Look for a repeated bottleneck
sections.body: Review a small sample of recent replays across several maps. Group observations, not speculative causes: inputs before arrival, losing rhythm after a burst, or leaving slider exits early. Record how often each demand occurred. A rare dramatic miss should not automatically outrank a smaller mistake present throughout most of your plays.

sections.title: Practice: run one experiment
sections.body: Suggested exercise: write a prediction before changing your practice. For example: practising burst entries at a manageable rate should reduce first-note errors on two check maps. Keep your usual setup fixed, collect a baseline and practise in a short planned block. Test the check maps again before rehearsing them. Changing your grip, skin, rate and map pool together makes the result difficult to interpret.

sections.title: Decide what to keep next session
sections.body: Keep an exercise when its intended observation improves repeatedly and transfers beyond the rehearsed pattern. Modify it when a different error becomes the limit. Drop it when repeated checks show no relevant change, rather than assuming more repetitions must work. Treat this as a practical review method, not a guaranteed schedule for rank gains. Preserve notes on unsuccessful experiments so you do not unknowingly repeat them.

guides.title: Missing jumps? Separate aim errors from early and late taps
guides.description: Diagnose overshoots, undershoots and aim-tap coordination, then choose a focused practice exercise.

sections.title: Start with three misses, not your worst miss
sections.body: Choose three recent attempts on one difficulty with identical mods and rate. Review a few objects before each miss at reduced playback speed. Record the object time, cursor position at the input and whether the cursor entered the target before or after that input. A miss alone cannot tell you whether spacing, timing or reading caused the error. If the replay cannot resolve the input clearly, mark it uncertain rather than prescribing an aim fix.

sections.title: Find the mistake you actually repeat
sections.body: If the cursor is short of the target at the tap and reaches it afterwards, compare early tapping with incomplete movement. If it travels beyond the target, inspect whether the tap happened during the crossing or after leaving. If the cursor reaches the target but departs before the tap, work on coordination rather than simply moving faster. These are observations about cursor and input order; they do not establish what your eyes or hands intended.

sections.title: Practice: controlled arrivals
sections.body: Suggested drill: choose a short jump section whose rhythm you can already tap comfortably. Play three attempts, concentrating on arriving at each target in time for the tap rather than rushing toward the next object. Reduce rate or spacing if nearly every jump breaks down, but change only one demand. Review the same misses afterwards. Count cursor-outside-at-input events as well as misses: a lucky pass is not the same as repeatable control.

sections.title: Check transfer before increasing difficulty
sections.body: Replay the original section at its original settings, then try a second map with comparable spacing and rhythm. Compare several attempts rather than only the best one. If the practised section improves but the second map does not, keep the drill but add more pattern variety. If inputs remain early despite more controlled arrivals, switch your next practice focus to timing instead of continuing to increase spacing.

sections.title: Watch and apply
sections.body: Tonehh's aim guide is an optional companion video. After watching, choose one idea to test against your own replay evidence. The exercises here are AimMod practice suggestions, not a transcript of the video or a guarantee that one aiming style works for everyone.

sources.title: Watch: Tonehh - osu! How to ACTUALLY improve your aim, Part 1

guides.title: Streams and bursts: find where your tapping breaks down
guides.description: Separate starting a burst, maintaining rhythm and aiming a stream before increasing speed or length.

sections.title: Compare the beginning and end of the pattern
sections.body: Review several bursts at the same rate. Does the first tap miss, does accuracy drift through the middle, or do extra taps continue after the pattern ends? Also check whether the cursor remains on the objects. A late first input followed by steady spacing is a different problem from inputs that progressively fall behind. Do not label every stream miss as insufficient speed.

sections.title: Use note spacing, not BPM alone
sections.body: BPM describes the musical tempo, not how many notes you must tap each second. Note subdivision matters: a quarter-beat stream and a half-beat pattern at the same BPM require different tapping rates. Compare subdivision, burst length, spacing and rate-changing mods together. Start with patterns you can distinguish visually and rhythmically before using them to assess sustained tapping.

sections.title: Practice: change length before speed
sections.body: Suggested drill: select short bursts at a comfortable fixed rate. Play a few attempts with attention to starting and stopping at the intended notes. Then compare slightly longer bursts at the same rate. If short bursts are consistent but longer ones deteriorate, work on maintaining the rhythm over length. If both fail at their first note, review the transition into the burst before increasing duration. Keep breaks between sets; stop a session rather than trying to push through discomfort.

sections.title: Keep a useful result log
sections.body: Record the map difficulty, rate, approximate burst length, accuracy and where the first error occurred. Compare a handful of fresh attempts on another day, not just repetitions immediately after memorising the section. Success means the same demand is more consistent across different patterns. A single high-speed pass or an improvement on only one memorised stream is not enough to establish that.

sources.title: Watch: osu! phd: a comprehensive introduction to every skill

guides.title: Turn your replay mistakes into a useful practice session
guides.description: Choose one recurring weakness, practise it in context and check improvement without chasing only your best score.

sections.title: Choose one question for today
sections.body: Use recent plays that reflect your current ability. Pick a recurring observation across multiple attempts: leaving circles before tapping, losing rhythm after a burst, or breaking down when a pattern becomes denser. Write a testable question such as: can I keep inputs on target through this transition? Avoid goals like improve everything or gain a fixed amount of PP in one session.

sections.title: Establish a baseline
sections.body: Choose two or three relevant maps and keep their difficulty, client, mods and rate fixed. Record a few attempts including failures. Note section misses and accuracy, not only the final score. Different patterns with similar stars are not interchangeable, so choose maps that actually contain the demand you want to test.

sections.title: Repeat the section with its lead-in
sections.body: Suggested drill: practise the difficult section with enough preceding objects to preserve the transition and rhythm. Use a short group of repetitions with breaks rather than immediately retrying indefinitely. Change one variable, such as rate, only when you cannot complete enough of the pattern to learn from it. Do not remove every lead-in object: hitting an isolated pattern is not the same task as entering it during a full play.

sections.title: Finish with a transfer check
sections.body: Return to the original settings for a complete attempt, then test a different map with the same demand. Compare the repeated error and the judgement breakdown with your baseline. Keep the exercise if both show improvement across attempts. If only the rehearsed section improves, add variation next time. If the error changes, update your practice question rather than repeating an exercise just because it once helped.

sections.title: Review the week, not only the personal best
sections.body: Compare recent sessions using the same settings and retain unsuccessful attempts. Look for fewer repeated errors and more consistent results before raising the challenge. Keep score targets separate from practice targets: one seeks a strong result with existing skills; the other deliberately exposes a weakness. Use PP as one result measure, not the only definition of a productive session.

sources.title: Watch: osu! phd: a comprehensive introduction to every skill

guides.title: osu! PP explained: star rating, score PP and profile gains
guides.description: Understand why a 200 PP play does not add 200 profile PP, compare realistic score scenarios, and troubleshoot differences between calculators.

sections.title: Which PP number are you looking at?
sections.body: Star rating is calculated difficulty, not a prediction of your result. Score PP evaluates a particular performance; profile PP combines weighted performances. Keep those three numbers separate. A calculator's SS scenario assumes a perfect result and is not a personal target by itself. Before comparing two estimates, check the exact difficulty, ruleset, mods and rate, then ask whether the assumed accuracy and misses resemble your recent complete attempts.

sections.title: Why a 200 PP play does not add 200 PP
sections.body: The weight for a score at position n in your best performances is 0.95^(n-1). A 200 PP score in second place contributes 190 weighted PP. That contribution is not the profile increase: inserting it can move other scores down, and a replacement changes an existing contribution. Bonus PP is separate. For a useful before-and-after comparison, record your profile total and the score's position instead of subtracting its raw PP from your new total.

sections.title: Build a realistic scenario before choosing a target
sections.body: Suggested comparison: take three recent complete attempts on one difficulty and note accuracy, misses and slider breaks. Calculate a scenario resembling the middle attempt, another resembling your best repeatable attempt, and SS. Keep the same calculator and settings. If only the SS number looks attractive while actual attempts repeatedly fail the ending, move that map into practice rather than treating its ceiling as expected earnings. Do not estimate PP by multiplying SS PP by accuracy or a compatibility percentage.

sections.title: Why do two calculators disagree?
sections.body: Check the difficulty ID and whether one tool used an edited beatmap. Next compare mod settings, clock rate, judgement assumptions and calculation version. Official difficulty and PP updates can change old values. Record whether a number is an official submitted result or an estimate. If a tool lacks the necessary score data, leave PP unavailable rather than substituting zero or copying the value from another play on the same map.

sections.title: Use PP without letting it choose every session
sections.body: Try two similarly rated difficulties with different patterns. Use the one you can already execute consistently for a score attempt; use a specific troublesome section from the other for practice. Revisit both after several sessions under the same settings. Better accuracy or fewer repeat errors can justify continuing the exercise even before a new top score appears. There is no universal star-to-PP conversion or guaranteed daily profile gain.

guides.title: How to review an osu! replay and diagnose repeated misses
guides.description: Follow a replay review checklist, separate aim and timing observations, and troubleshoot missing beatmaps or incomplete score data.

sections.title: Start with the right replay and difficulty
sections.body: Match the player, play time, exact difficulty and mods before reviewing. A score summary is not a cursor replay: accuracy and miss count cannot reconstruct movement or key presses. An exported .osr also needs its matching beatmap. If playback cannot locate the map, obtain the original difficulty instead of substituting another difficulty with the same song title. In stable, the results screen's F2 export is the documented way to save a replay.

sections.title: Review a short sequence, not a frozen miss
sections.body: Choose three errors, including one from an unsuccessful attempt. Watch each lead-in at normal speed, then slow playback to inspect the input and movement order. Note the object time, cursor position when input occurs, and the next object. Example note: at 01:12, the cursor is left of the circle on input and enters it afterwards. This supports an arrival/tap coordination observation; it does not prove that sensitivity, reaction time or reading is the cause.

sections.title: Turn the observation into the next check
sections.body: Cursor outside on input: inspect whether movement stops short or continues past the target. Cursor reaches the target before the input: check whether it leaves too soon. No clear input: inspect recorded key state rather than assuming an aim error. For sliders, locate the head, tick, repeat or end involved before comparing failures. If playback or analysis cannot resolve the event, mark it unknown. Do not count an uncertain label as a confirmed technique problem.

sections.title: Choose one correction you can test
sections.body: Suggested exercise: after finding the same observation in several places, choose a short section that contains the preceding object and the next transition. Make three attempts with one focus, such as keeping the cursor on the target until the intended tap. Then play another section with comparable movement and rhythm. Record whether the original error decreased and whether a new error appeared. A clean memorised section alone is not evidence of reliable transfer.

sections.title: When replay review cannot answer the question
sections.body: If a replay ends early, review only the portion actually recorded. If a download is unavailable, a public score entry does not guarantee accessible replay bytes. If the cursor looks wrong after an import, first compare the original map and mod settings. Avoid deleting the original replay while troubleshooting. Keep a compact log: difficulty ID, time, observed event, uncertainty and next check. That gives the next review a concrete starting point.

guides.title: osu! jump, burst or stream practice: choose the right maps
guides.description: Build a practice pool around spacing, note rate and pattern length, with examples for selecting a manageable challenge and testing progress.

sections.title: Describe the section before searching for maps
sections.body: Jumps emphasise movement between separated targets; streams commonly place circles in quick succession, often on quarter-beat subdivisions. A burst is a short sequence rather than a guarantee of one fixed length. For your own search, write the demand explicitly: wide jumps at a comfortable rhythm, five-note burst entries, or longer low-spacing sequences. A map called a stream map may still fail to contain the particular transition you need.

sections.title: Use three filters instead of one star range
sections.body: Compare spacing, note interval and sequence length. At 180 BPM, regularly spaced quarter-beat notes arrive every 83.3 milliseconds, or 12 per second; half-beat notes arrive every 166.7 milliseconds, or 6 per second. These are interval calculations, not a prescription to tap faster. A short and a long sequence can share the same interval but present different challenges. Star rating is a starting filter, not a substitute for inspecting the relevant section.

sections.title: Match the exercise to the repeated observation
sections.body: If jumps fail while their rhythm remains comfortable, try a similar rhythm with less spacing. If the first note of a burst repeatedly fails but later notes are clean, include the preceding object rather than practising only the middle of the burst. If errors accumulate later in a sequence, compare a shorter sequence at the same rate. If the cursor loses a direction change while tapping stays regular, select a less demanding turn rather than changing every setting.

sections.title: Build a pool with an easier step and a transfer check
sections.body: Suggested pool: one manageable example, one current challenge and one unfamiliar map sharing the target demand. For example, compare three-, five- and seven-note bursts near one comfortable tempo instead of adding speed and length together. Play a fresh baseline on each. Practise the challenge briefly, then return to the original settings and the unfamiliar map. The numbers are an example progression, not a required definition of difficulty.

sections.title: Know when to replace a practice map
sections.body: Move to a harder variation after you can repeat the intended section and retain that control on another map, not merely after one pass. Step back if almost every attempt fails before reaching the target section. Replace a map when its unrelated patterns dominate your errors or extensive repetition has turned the exercise into memorisation. Keep the old map as an occasional check, with the exact difficulty and rate recorded.

guides.title: osu! stable vs lazer: accuracy, sliders and Classic explained
guides.description: Troubleshoot accuracy and score differences after switching to lazer, distinguish Classic mod from score display, and compare matched plays.

sections.title: A client change can change what the result measures
sections.body: In ordinary stable gameplay, a successful slider head has more forgiving accuracy requirements than a hit circle. Lazer judges slider-head timing; ScoreV2 and Classic settings require separate consideration. If accuracy drops mainly on slider-heavy maps after switching, inspect head judgements before concluding that all of your timing deteriorated. Treat circle-only sections as a useful comparison, not as proof that the clients behave identically.

sections.title: Classic mod is not classic score display
sections.body: Lazer's Classic mod restores selected legacy behaviours. Its classic score display is a different setting: it changes how score totals are presented, not a switch back to stable's complete gameplay rules. The official migration guide also documents grading changes that Classic does not undo. Compare the actual mod settings, judgements and scoring display rather than assuming that matching the word Classic makes two results interchangeable.

sections.title: Troubleshoot one difference at a time
sections.body: First confirm the exact beatmap version, then record rate, AR, OD and enabled mod settings. Next check audio and input settings against your old setup; do not assume migration copied every preference. Choose a familiar difficulty with both circles and sliders. Compare several attempts and note whether the change appears throughout the map or mainly on slider entries. Avoid changing offset, skin and mod settings together, which would obscure the comparison.

sections.title: Use a small comparison sheet
sections.body: Suggested columns: client, score date, difficulty ID, mods with settings, displayed score type, accuracy, misses and slider-head observations. Keep a stable play, a lazer play and any Classic experiment on separate rows. If only raw score differs, first check the score display rather than treating it as lost skill. If circle judgements remain similar but slider heads worsen, practise their entries and check another slider-heavy map before judging progress.

sections.title: Keep original results and current documentation
sections.body: An imported old play is not a new performance under your current setup. Preserve its original context and avoid averaging it with new attempts to make a single accuracy trend. For progress, compare a consistent group of plays within one setup, then describe cross-client differences separately. Use the official migration guide for current compatibility details; an old video or feature checklist may describe a different lazer release.

sources.title: osu! help centre: Upgrading to lazer

guides.title: osu! practice rates and mods: BPM, timing and useful notes
guides.description: Calculate effective BPM for DT, HT and custom rates, record the settings that matter, and test whether slower practice transfers to normal speed.

sections.title: DT is not twice as fast, and HT is not half speed
sections.body: Standard Double Time uses 1.5x speed; standard Half Time uses 0.75x. Calculate effective BPM as original BPM multiplied by clock rate. A 180 BPM section becomes 270 BPM at 1.5x and 135 BPM at 0.75x. For a constant-rate 120-second section, duration becomes 80 seconds or 160 seconds respectively. These examples describe elapsed time, not an automatic PP multiplier or a guarantee of ranked eligibility.

sections.title: Keep the exact rate, not just the mod name
sections.body: When using a custom rate, write the actual value beside the mod acronym. Keep the difficulty ID, client, AR, OD and other changed settings in the same note. Example: original 180 BPM, rate 0.90x, effective 162 BPM, same difficulty and skin. For a map with tempo changes, apply the rate to each relevant section rather than treating one BPM label as a complete description of the map.

sections.title: A slower section is not an aim-only experiment
sections.body: Changing clock rate changes the time between objects and the real time available for reading and hitting them. It can make several demands easier at once. If a slowed attempt improves, that alone does not identify the original problem. Compare the cursor and input sequence to see what changed. Do not multiply the AR or OD number by the rate as if these difficulty settings were BPM; use the client's effective settings when available.

sections.title: Practise below the target, then retest the target
sections.body: Suggested exercise: take one baseline at 1.00x, then try the same troublesome section at a manageable lower rate while keeping its lead-in. Make a small set of attempts and record the first repeated error. Increase the rate only when the intended movement and rhythm remain repeatable; return to 1.00x for a check before ending. If the lower rate is clean but the target is unchanged, use an intermediate step or an easier section rather than counting the slowed score as the target result.

sections.title: Why does my estimate or leaderboard result differ?
sections.body: Compare every mod setting, not only the visible acronym, and ensure the calculator used the same difficulty and rate. Check current eligibility in the client instead of assuming that a displayed PP estimate promises submission or ranking. Keep practice attempts and submitted score targets distinguishable in your notes. The useful outcome is a repeatable change at the intended settings, not a larger number produced by changing the task.

guides.title: osu! accuracy vs combo: why a cleaner play can score less
guides.description: Understand 300s, 100s, misses and full combo with a worked accuracy example, then compare complete attempts without confusing score and PP.

sections.title: Accuracy measures judgement value, not just hit percentage
sections.body: For an osu!standard example containing only 100 hit circles, 90 GREATs and 10 OKs give (90 x 300 + 10 x 100) / (100 x 300) = 93.33% accuracy. All circles were hit, but some received less than full value. By contrast, 99 GREATs and one miss give 99% despite the combo break. This worked example is not a formula to apply blindly to slider events or another ruleset.

sections.title: Zero misses does not always mean full combo
sections.body: A maximum-combo result and a zero-miss result are not always interchangeable. Slider breaks or dropped ends can prevent maximum combo without appearing as ordinary circle misses, depending on the scoring rules. Community shorthand around dropped ends can also differ from the strict maximum-combo definition. Check the actual combo and slider judgements before labelling a play FC. A full combo is not automatically SS: lower-value judgements can still reduce accuracy.

sections.title: A lower score can contain a useful improvement
sections.body: Suggested comparison: attempt A has fewer lower-value judgements but one late-map combo break; attempt B has more lower-value judgements but a longer combo. Do not pick a universal winner from accuracy or score alone. For an accuracy exercise, compare timing judgements in the target section. For a consistency goal, compare repeated breaks across full plays. For a PP target, use the actual performance calculation rather than treating score or combo as a substitute.

sections.title: Check completion and scoring context first
sections.body: Before comparing totals, match difficulty, client, mods and rate. Check whether both attempts reached the same section. A 99% result that ended before the hardest pattern does not demonstrate better full-map accuracy than a 97% completion. Also distinguish a displayed score number from PP. When one result comes from another client or score-display mode, establish a compatible comparison before drawing a progression trend.

sections.title: Use a result log that leads to a decision
sections.body: For three full attempts, record accuracy, judgement counts, misses, maximum combo and the first troublesome section. Add a brief observation rather than only a final percentage: burst entry early, slider exit broken, or cause unclear. Next session, keep the settings fixed and compare that same observation. Continue the exercise when it improves repeatedly; change focus when another error becomes the limit. Keep the failed attempts visible so the comparison reflects typical play.

guides.title: Small circles: practise precision without changing everything
guides.description: Separate small-target precision from jump speed, then test controlled arrivals with a repeatable osu! practice exercise.

sections.title: Check target size before blaming your speed
sections.body: In osu!standard, higher circle size (CS) makes circles and sliders smaller. The same cursor movement can therefore succeed on one difficulty and miss on another even when the object centres are equally far apart. Treat CS as a separate practice variable, not a synonym for star rating. Start with a section where the next object is easy to identify and the rhythm is comfortable; otherwise a reading or tapping error can look like a precision problem.

sections.title: Compare the press position, not only the cursor trail
sections.body: Choose three misses and inspect where the cursor was when the relevant input occurred. Passing through a circle before or after the press does not make that input an aimed hit. Note whether you repeatedly stop short, move beyond the far edge, or pass to one side. Also keep an example that succeeded. If both examples use a similar movement but the press arrives at different times, test aim-tap coordination before changing your sensitivity.

sections.title: Set up a controlled comparison
sections.body: Suggested exercise: pick a comfortable difficulty with moderate spacing and a mix of directions. Keep your device settings, skin, approach rate and playback rate fixed. If you make a practice copy with a different CS, label it clearly and retain the original. Do not use Hard Rock as a CS-only experiment: it changes other difficulty settings as well. Record the effective CS and whether you played the original or an edited copy.

sections.title: Practise a short sequence of arrivals
sections.body: Select a phrase of roughly eight to sixteen circles with a clear lead-in. Play it at a demand where you can still choose your movement instead of reacting in a panic. Aim for a deliberate arrival at each target and let the rhythm determine the press; do not wait for a perfect visual centre and then tap late. After three attempts, review the same two transitions in each replay. If errors increase, simplify spacing before making targets smaller again.

sections.title: Look for a repeatable direction-specific error
sections.body: A useful note is specific: 'three of five down-left arrivals stopped short at the press' is more actionable than 'bad aim'. Compare that direction with successful movements of similar distance. Do not infer a faulty tablet area from a single miss, and do not let one successful attempt settle the question. If you later test a device setting, save its old value and repeat the comparison separately from the CS exercise.

sections.title: Finish on the original and an unfamiliar map
sections.body: Return to the unedited difficulty, then try a second map with comparable target size and spacing. Count off-target presses in the chosen phrases rather than judging the experiment only by total accuracy. Improvement on the edited phrase alone may reflect familiarity. A useful next step is fewer precision errors on the original without a new increase in late hits. Keep the smaller-circle exercise as practice, not as a requirement to change your normal settings.

sources.title: Further viewing: pishifat - osu!mapping: circle size

guides.title: Alternating: practise the entry and exit, not just the stream
guides.description: Use short, comfortable patterns to diagnose finger-order mistakes when switching between single taps, bursts and alternating.

sections.title: Choose the tapping behaviour you want to learn
sections.body: Alternating distributes successive taps between two inputs. Single-tapping mainly uses one input, with many players switching to two for faster sequences. You do not need to declare one style universally better before practising a difficult transition. Choose a concrete goal such as starting a three-note burst with either finger, or alternating a simple phrase without accidentally pressing twice with the same finger. Keep your normal style available for ordinary play.

sections.title: Find the first input that differs from your plan
sections.body: Watch a replay's key overlay alongside the objects. Does the error happen when entering the burst, halfway through it, or on the first circle after it? A burst followed by an accidental extra press is a different problem from a burst that starts late. Input states help you locate the event, but they do not measure physical finger force or prove that a particular finger is weak. Write down the sequence you intended before interpreting the replay.

sections.title: Start with an easy rhythm and familiar aim
sections.body: Suggested exercise: select a short phrase whose spacing and speed already feel comfortable. Alternate one press per object, then repeat the phrase beginning with the other input. Review whether the intended order survived, not whether the attempt produced a personal best. If the movement itself is difficult, choose a simpler map. The purpose is to make finger order observable; a pattern that immediately turns into uncontrolled tapping is not a useful starting test.

sections.title: Include the object after the burst
sections.body: Next, practise a single note, a short burst and the following note as one phrase. Under strict alternation, three successive taps starting on K1 end on K1; the next tap would be K2. Four taps end on K2, leaving K1 next. This is an example sequence, not a rule that every player must follow. Use it to check whether an odd- or even-length burst changes your intended exit. Keep the gap after the burst in the exercise.

sections.title: Change order before adding more speed
sections.body: Try a few phrases with different burst lengths while keeping the pace manageable. Record an entry error, an internal ordering error or an exit error for each attempt. Only increase demand after you can reproduce the intended sequence across more than one phrase. Do not turn this into a maximum-tapping test or force a new finger position because a stronger player uses it. Stop an exercise that causes discomfort rather than trying to finish a quota.

sections.title: Check whether the new option helps normal play
sections.body: Finish with an unfamiliar, comfortable map and play normally. Look for the transition you practised, without trying to police every input for the whole song. If deliberate alternation works only in the isolated phrase, keep the next session short and focused on transfer. If both entry choices work, use the one that lets you follow the music reliably. The result you want is a usable option at a difficult transition, not a particular-looking key overlay.

sources.title: osu! wiki: Play style and input overlays

guides.title: Rhythm changes: recognise subdivisions and leave room for rests
guides.description: Learn to distinguish note count from rhythm, locate rushed transitions and practise changing subdivisions without adding extra taps.

sections.title: Three objects do not automatically mean triplet timing
sections.body: Object count tells you how many taps a circle pattern needs, not how those taps are spaced in time. A three-object burst can use evenly spaced quarter-beat intervals without being a musical triplet. In osu!'s editor, 1/4 snapping divides one beat into four equal parts; 1/3 divides it into three. A pattern can also leave some positions empty. Inspect the intervals before deciding to practise the entire section as a faster version of your usual tapping.

sections.title: Use one beat as a timing reference
sections.body: For a section timed at 120 BPM, one beat lasts 500 milliseconds. An interval of one quarter of that beat is 125 milliseconds; one third is about 166.7 milliseconds. These are examples, not speed targets. They illustrate why similar-looking groups can require different timing. Use the actual timing section and playback rate for your map. A song's headline BPM is not enough to describe every interval you will encounter.

sections.title: Listen to the phrase before repeating it
sections.body: Suggested exercise: choose a short section where your accuracy drops as the rhythm changes. Listen once without trying to play and identify a steady pulse. Then follow the mapped objects against that pulse. Ask which sounds the objects follow and where there is a deliberate gap. Do not assume every audible drum or vocal syllable requires a press. If you cannot yet describe the rhythm, examine the object timeline before adding more attempts.

sections.title: Practise the change, including silence
sections.body: Play a phrase that contains the comfortable rhythm, the change and the next few objects. Keep the aim demand easy enough that tapping is the question being tested. Watch for continuing the previous tap rate into a longer gap, or adding a press after a short burst has ended. Repeat the whole phrase rather than starting immediately on its hardest object. If you reduce playback rate, note the rate and return to the original for a separate comparison.

sections.title: Find where the timing first drifts
sections.body: Review the first mistimed input, not just the final miss. If the new rhythm begins correctly but your taps gradually move early, try maintaining the new spacing through the whole group. If the first object is already late, practise recognising the transition from its lead-in. If there is an extra tap in the rest, include that gap in your next exercise. A single timing histogram for the whole map can conceal these different patterns.

sections.title: Transfer the rhythm to different spacing
sections.body: Choose a second map with a comparable rhythm change but different object positions. Keep the speed comfortable and check whether you can recognise the change without memorising the first map's cursor path. Then return to ordinary play. Success means the rhythm remains controlled through the transition and rest, not merely that you survived by pressing more often. For a mapping perspective on rhythm choice, pishifat's basic rhythm episode is listed below as further viewing.

sources.title: Further viewing: pishifat - osu!mapping: basic rhythm

guides.title: Choose an osu! skin by what you can read during play
guides.description: Compare circle numbers, approach circles, slider tracking and cursor contrast with a practical skin-readability test.

sections.title: Test gameplay elements, not only the preview image
sections.body: A skin changes the presentation of gameplay elements; an attractive menu does not tell you whether you can follow a crowded phrase. Pick a familiar map with separate circles, overlapping objects and at least one reversing slider. Compare the specific cues you use: object numbers, the approach circle, the slider ball and the cursor. Keep the same map and settings while checking two skins so that a different song or difficulty does not decide the comparison for you.

sections.title: Check which skin is actually being displayed
sections.body: The stable client has separate options for beatmap skins, the skin cursor and sound samples. A map can therefore change part of what you see or hear even after you select a skin. Check those options before concluding that a skin behaves inconsistently. Setting names and layout can differ in lazer. Save your starting configuration so that each change is reversible, and keep the audio choice fixed while you compare visuals.

sections.title: Run a four-cue readability check
sections.body: Suggested exercise: pause a replay before a busy phrase and answer four questions. Can you identify the next object number? Can you distinguish its approach circle from nearby outlines? Can you locate the slider ball rather than just the slider body? Can you see the cursor against both bright and dark parts of the scene? Resume at normal speed afterwards. A still image is useful for locating contrast problems, but the final test is whether those cues remain clear while moving.

sections.title: Adjust one source of visual competition
sections.body: If a background obscures objects, test a different dim level before replacing the entire skin. If the cursor covers a target number, compare a modest cursor-size adjustment while leaving target size unchanged. If effects draw attention away from upcoming objects, test the relevant visual option on the same phrase. Do not change approach rate at the same time: that would change how long objects are visible, rather than only how clearly you can distinguish them.

sections.title: Compare two short plays without chasing a record
sections.body: Play the same comfortable map once with each candidate skin, then reverse the order on another map. Note concrete problems such as losing the cursor at a slider exit or confusing adjacent numbers. A higher score on the second attempt may come from familiarity, so use more than one map and do not judge only the best attempt. Keep a skin that makes your recurring problem easier to observe and handle, even if its results-screen artwork is less appealing.

sections.title: Keep a dependable baseline
sections.body: Once you have a readable setup, save its skin name and relevant settings in your practice notes. Return to it when testing unfamiliar maps, and reserve further visual changes for a specific problem you can reproduce. A skin cannot establish that you have fixed a rhythm or movement error simply because the play looks cleaner. Use the replay to check the original mistake again. The aim is a clear, repeatable view of the task rather than a promise of extra PP.

sources.title: osu! wiki: osu! gameplay skin elements

guides.title: Hear your timing: balance hitsounds and music before practising
guides.description: Check which sounds follow your inputs, compare music and effect balance, and avoid mistaking an audio change for a timing fix.

sections.title: Separate the song from input feedback
sections.body: Hitsounds provide feedback when you interact with hit objects. A circle or slider-head sound can help you hear how your input lines up with the music. Not every sound is a fresh keypress, though: slider events can produce passive sounds, and storyboard samples can play independently of whether you hit an object. Before using a sound to diagnose timing, establish which event produced it. Treat the replay's input and judgement data as a separate check.

sections.title: Start with a simple, audible comparison
sections.body: Suggested exercise: choose a familiar map with a clear pulse and a simple circle section. Keep the output device, playback rate and timing offsets unchanged. Listen to the phrase once, then play it while attending to the relationship between the music and your circle hitsounds. If you cannot distinguish the two, first adjust their balance rather than changing universal offset. Lowering the competing channel may make the cue clearer without increasing the overall volume.

sections.title: Know what the volume controls change
sections.body: In stable, music and effect volume are separate controls; the effect channel includes hitsounds and other game sounds. Skin and beatmap sound settings also affect which samples you hear. Record the selected skin and whether beatmap samples are being used. Client layouts can differ, so look for the equivalent controls in your version. Avoid copying someone else's percentages as a target: different samples and output setups can produce very different balances at the same displayed values.

sections.title: Compare two balances on the same phrase
sections.body: Make a small balance change, play the phrase again, then return to the original balance for a third attempt. Ask whether the pulse is still audible and whether you can hear a deliberately observed early or late hit against it. Check the judgement result afterwards instead of assuming that a sharper-sounding sample means better timing. If one balance helps only because you have memorised the phrase, repeat the comparison on a second comfortable song.

sections.title: Do not use a slider sound as proof of a new tap
sections.body: A repeated sound during a slider may be feedback from following its path rather than an instruction to press again. Review a circle-only phrase first if that distinction is confusing, then compare a phrase with sliders while watching the input overlay. Keep track of the slider head and the next circle separately. Pishifat's hitsounds episode is included as further viewing from a mapping perspective; the exercise here is to identify the cues in your own play, not to imitate a particular sample set.

sections.title: Keep audio clarity and calibration as separate questions
sections.body: After choosing an audible balance, play several familiar maps with unchanged offsets. Record whether the new balance helps you notice a recurring error, rather than claiming it corrected that error automatically. If timing still seems consistently displaced, investigate that separately using comparable plays and the client's calibration tools. Do not repeatedly move an offset to rescue one difficult section. Save a dependable audio setup and spend the next practice block on the specific rhythm or input mistake that remains.
